summary: For learners aged 11–12: build absolute value as distance from zero on the number line (always ≥0, so |−5| = |5| = 5), interpret it as magnitude in real contexts (size of a debt, depth below sea level), and keep it sharply separate from ordering (−7 < −3 but |−7| > |−3|). Read |x| aloud as 'the distance of x from zero', not 'make it positive'. A manipulable number line is the core activity; an annotated static line, a consolidation set of short items, and a context dialogue are supporting approaches with distinct purposes.
misconceptions: Believing |x| just 'removes the minus sign' as a symbol trick rather than measuring distance (fails for expressions like |x−3|)
Thinking the number with the greater absolute value is automatically the greater number (−9 > −2)
Assuming absolute value can be negative

activities.title: Measure distance from zero on a draggable number line
steps: Drag a point along a number line and watch a glowing arc from 0 to the point report its length as |x|, which is positive on either side of zero and is 0 only when the point is at zero.
Park the point at −5, then flip on a mirror toggle so the reflection at +5 lays down an identical arc — observe |−5| = |5| = 5.

Read a twin read-out that shows the signed value beside its absolute value; move the point to −9 then to −2 and notice the arc for −9 is LONGER even though −9 sits further LEFT (is the smaller number).
Drag the point across zero and watch the |x| read-out shrink to 0 and climb again — distance tracks how far from zero, never which side.
activities.insight: Absolute value is a distance (a length) from zero: it is never negative, two symmetric points share one absolute value, and 'further from zero' is a different question from 'greater number'.

activities.title: Annotated number line with distance arcs (static anchor)
steps: On a number line, mark −5 and 5 and draw the arc from 0 to each, confirming both measure 5 units.
Reveal a callout that contrasts the order statement (−5 < 5) with the magnitude statement (|−5| = |5|).
For a second pair such as −9 and −2, draw both arcs and state separately which number is greater (−2) and which has the greater absolute value (−9).
activities.insight: Even without live movement, measuring arcs from zero establishes 'distance from zero' and the idea that two different numbers can share one absolute value.

activities.title: Consolidation: evaluate and discriminate
steps: Match signed values to their absolute values.
Judge paired true/false statements such as '−9 > −2' (false) versus '|−9| > |−2|' (true), and explain each by the number line.
activities.insight: Once the distance meaning is built, learners can reliably compute absolute values and tell absolute-value comparisons apart from ordering comparisons.

activities.title: Context talk: larger debt vs larger number
steps: Discuss a scenario: 'You owe £40, I owe £15 — whose debt is bigger, and whose balance is the greater number?'
Explain that −40 is the larger debt (greater magnitude) yet the smaller/lower balance (−40 < −15).
Try a second context (−8°C vs −3°C, or a diver at −8 m vs −3 m): name who is deeper/colder/further from zero and whose value is the greater number.
activities.insight: In real contexts, magnitude (how far from zero) and order (which value is greater) answer different questions, and conflating them produces errors like '−40 is the greater number'.

checkQuestion: Ask: 'Which is the greater number, −8 or −3? And which has the greater absolute value? How do you know?'
checkAnswer: −3 is the greater number (it is closer to zero / further right on the number line). But −8 has the greater absolute value, because |−8| = 8 and |−3| = 3 — absolute value is distance from zero, ignoring direction.
